prerequisites: Well-established knowledge of Mathematical Analysis, Linear Algebra and Geometry, particularly in complex numbers, differential and integral calculus, and vector spaces.
Prior passing of the Mathematical Analysis and Linear Algebra and Geometry courses is strongly recommended.

learning_outcomes.text: Know the terminology related to signals and systems (discrete-time and continuous-time).
Know and understand the basic principles of generalized signals (Dirac delta or impulse).
Know and understand the tools of Fourier analysis for signals and systems.
Know and understand the tools for solving linear ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients.
Apply advanced mathematical tools to represent and analyze signals of various nature (continuous-time or discrete-time, periodic or aperiodic).
Identify and describe the properties of transformations and systems, particularly linear time-invariant systems.
Use Fourier analysis to interpret signals and systems in the frequency domain and understand their spectral characteristics.
Master the concepts of impulse response, frequency response, and transfer function of a linear time-invariant system.
Analyze the consequences of sampling and design procedures for the reconstruction of continuous signals from discrete data.
Solve differential and difference equations in the time domain and with Laplace and Z-transforms, interpreting the results in engineering contexts.
Use computational scripts for the analysis of signals and systems, with particular attention to graphical representation and spectral evaluation.
Evaluate the most appropriate tools for analyzing and designing linear time-invariant systems.
Explain theoretical concepts and problem-solving approaches using appropriate technical language and clear logical reasoning in written format.

syllabus_topics: Review of complex arithmetic and analysis
Definition of signal spaces of interest: L-1, L-2, L-infinity (in continuous and discrete time)
Periodic signals: sinusoid and pure imaginary exponential
Dirac delta, generalized functions, generalized derivatives
Definition of system and notable systems (affine time transformations)
Convolution in discrete and continuous time
Amplitude and phase response of an LTI
Signals and Systems in the Frequency Domain
Fourier Series: pure imaginary exponentials in harmonic relation, fundamental theorems of Fourier series (Riesz-Fischer and Dirichlet)
Calculation of Fourier coefficients for notable signals
Isomorphism between periodic signals in discrete time and Euclidean space C^N
Fourier Transform: definition and calculation examples
Inversion theorems in L-1 and L-2
Systems in the frequency domain: LTI as frequency product
Discrete-time Fourier Transform (DTFT): definition, properties, relation with DFT (zero-padding)
Sampling of continuous-time signals: Poisson's formula, sampling theorem, ideal interpolation formula (sinc)
Linear Ordinary Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients
Main theorems: existence and uniqueness of the solution of a Cauchy problem, structure of solutions of an LODECC
One-sided LT and application to the causal Cauchy problem
Introduction to the Z-transform and difference equations
Introduction to software environments for scientific computing (ex. Python, Matlab)
Guided experimentation on mathematical models of signals and systems
Computational applications for harmonic analysis and the study of frequency-domain behavior
Selected case studies within the field of signal theory and LTI systems
teaching_methods: Use of technological tools (moodle and/or other educational tools, software, videos, quizzes, wooclap)
In-depth lectures on mathematical aspects alternating with the solution of exercises
Computer-based applied activities through guided demonstrations and interactive sessions
Shared problem-solving, engaging students through guided analysis of case studies and in-class resolution of specific problems

assessment_methods.method: Closed-book written test (theoretical questions and exercises)

assessment_rules: The exam consists of a closed-book written test and an oral examination. The written test includes theoretical questions and exercises to assess mastery of techniques and application in engineering contexts. The oral examination completes the assessment of theoretical principles and their application. The use of generative artificial intelligence tools is not allowed during the exam or for assignments.
